I have experience coding in Python, Java, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, so I can contribute to both the backend logic and the web interface. summary: Our project, Flame in Freefall, will provide an intelligent dashboard for organizing, summarizing, ranking and analyzing NASA microgravity combustion experiments using SI technology. The dashboard would aid users in discovering patterns and understanding possible fire-safety hazards in NASA microgravity combustion experiments.Instead of merely presenting scientific information, our purpose is to apply these scientific findings to practical uses. Through simplifying NASA discoveries, we would like to assist scientists and engineers in creating more safe spacecrafts, finding ways to prevent fires, and ensuring astronaut safety on future expeditions. Space exploration in the future does not only entail how far man travels, but how safe he gets there as well. This is what we aspire to accomplish using the Interstellar Embers through knowledge gained from years of experience in NASA.
details:
What the project does and how it works =

Research on fire safety in space often remains buried beneath layers of dense technical records, scattered across isolated archives that require painstaking, one-by-one examination. InterstellarEmbers brings NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) research to the surface, gathering bundled investigation data into a single, browser-based workspace designed for clear exploration.

The dashboard connects four distinct lenses for examining the archive: a habitat-risk and PSI-ranking view, a cross-investigation dataset matrix, flame-physics and benchmark visualizations, and an offline PSI Fire Safety Co-Pilot. Rather than forcing users to navigate disconnected tools, this structure allows them to trace a path from a mission scenario straight to the relevant investigations and the raw records beneath them. Within the mission-profile view, users can adjust the core conditions that govern flame behavior—oxygen concentration, cabin pressure, airflow, and gravity regime—testing scenarios across preset environments like the ISS, an Artemis Moon Base, a Lunar Gateway or Rover, and an xEMU EVA spacesuit. The resulting risk index serves as an exploratory compass rather than a validated operational forecast. From there, the research matrix opens up the archive itself, enabling users to filter investigations by ID or name and inspect original source fields instead of relying solely on surface-level charts. Completing the workspace, the Co-Pilot searches locally across the bundled PSI material, ranking relevant fields and assembling summaries tied directly to named datasets—operating without generative AI, external APIs, or a network connection, and refusing to fabricate an answer when the evidence is absent.

Benefits and intended impact =

Specialized aerospace research carries a steep barrier to entry, often leaving valuable experimental findings out of reach for those outside the immediate field. By pairing a visual dashboard and searchable matrix with plain-language summaries, InterstellarEmbers helps students, educators, and early mission planners orient themselves within complex data and identify which records warrant deeper study.

Above all, the platform is built to cultivate verification rather than blind trust. Every search result anchors its summary to specific PSI datasets and source fields, while the matrix keeps the underlying experimental records visible and accessible. Its purpose is to illuminate the research—not replace it. While it supports education and early planning discussions around how fire behaves in off-world habitats, it draws a firm boundary around operational safety: it is neither a flight-certified system nor an emergency guide, and the interface explicitly directs users to verify source records and follow approved onboard procedures and crew leadership in any real crisis.

Tools and technologies =

InterstellarEmbers is built with JavaScript and JSX using React, paired with Vite for development and bundling, and styled through CSS. Lucide React supplies the interface iconography, while all charts and visualizations render directly within the application. Because the PSI records are normalized and bundled locally into the build, the dashboard’s search and summary capabilities run entirely offline, keeping queries self-contained without relying on external servers. Running the project requires no specialized equipment beyond a standard web browser; while spacecraft and experimental hardware appear throughout the records as research context, they remain subjects of study rather than physical devices controlled by the software.

What makes the project creative and what the team considered =

The creative foundation of the project lies in uniting a deep research archive with a mission-driven interface. Instead of treating habitat modeling, data visualization, and archival search as separate tasks, InterstellarEmbers weaves them into a single, continuous workflow. Equally deliberate was the decision to build the Co-Pilot for transparency rather than black-box generation—ranking and citing local evidence directly so users can see precisely what matched their inquiry and follow that trail back to the original record.

Throughout development, the team accounted for the intricate interplay of variables that shape combustion in space—balancing oxygen levels, cabin pressure, airflow, and gravity alongside fuels, materials, detection, and suppression—while framing them as dimensions for inquiry rather than substitutes for formal engineering validation. Practical access and safety boundaries guided every choice: offline functionality removes barriers of connectivity and external dependencies, visible citations reinforce disciplined verification, and clear disclaimers preserve the distinction between research exploration and certified mission operations.
